passage: Rekha's thumb hovered over the share button. The video showed a crowd and a red caption: "THEY are coming for us. Share before it gets deleted!" Her chest was hot, and she wanted the whole class group to see it. Then she noticed the account had posted eleven angry videos that day, each ending with a link to buy a "support badge". Her cousin Charu was on the sofa. "Didi, look at this." Charu read the caption. "Where was it filmed?" "It doesn't say." "Then how do we know it's true? Whoever made this wants us furious." Rekha lowered the phone, searched for the clip, and found a news site saying it was from another city, years ago. She didn't share it.

qa.q: How many angry videos had the account posted that day?
qa.a: The account had posted eleven angry videos that day.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as her thumb hovered over share?
qa.a: Rekha felt angry, with a hot chest, and wanted the whole class group to see the clip.

qa.q: What could Rekha do before sharing anything similar?
qa.a: Pause, ask where and when it was filmed, and check a news source before passing it on.

qa.q: Why might the account owner want Rekha to be furious?
qa.a: The account posted many angry videos with a link to buy a badge, which suggests anger brings attention and money.

grounding: Memes and videos push Rekha to hate a group and share outrage; a pause and a check show it was made to anger and was old.

passage:
Monday. Dolma's feed was full of it: a video of a man shouting in a market, with a caption blaming "those outsiders" for everything wrong in the city. Then memes. Then more videos. By night her chest felt hot and tight. She had her thumb on "share to class group."

Wednesday. At lunch, she showed Gopika. "Look what they're doing to our city!" Gopika watched it twice. "Where's this from? The video says Pune, but the signboards are in another language." Dolma hadn't noticed. They searched together. The clip was from two years ago, in another state, about a road accident argument. The page that posted it sold T-shirts with angry slogans and had a donate button.

Friday. Dolma scrolled past three more memes. She felt the same flash of anger, and this time she noticed it like a warning light. She didn't share anything. Instead she asked Gopika, "Who makes money from me being this angry?" They spent the free period looking up how to check where a video comes from.

qa.q: What did the page that posted the clip sell?
qa.a: The page sold T-shirts with angry slogans and had a donate button.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: Dolma felt angry and tense, with a hot, tight chest, and almost shared the video with her class group.

qa.q: What changed in how Dolma handled the memes on Friday?
qa.a: Dolma treated her anger as a warning sign, did not share, and asked who profits from it, then learned how to check a video's source.

qa.q: How did Gopika help Dolma see the video differently?
qa.a: Gopika noticed the signboards did not match the city and suggested checking, which showed the clip was old and from somewhere else.

grounding: It shows a teen pushed by memes and videos to hate a group and share outrage, learning to recognise content built for profit and to pause and verify before sharing.

passage:
Vikas, you forward things fast, I've seen it. Let your Uday Mama tell you about one evening when I was seventeen.

There was a forward on the family chat. A blurry video, men with sticks, and a message: "They are coming to our area tonight. Share with everyone to warn them." Names of a community. My blood boiled. I was sure it was true. I had typed "Share to all" before I even thought.

Your Nani stopped me. She was watching over my shoulder. "Who sent this first?" I didn't know. "Where was it filmed?" I didn't know. "Why does it want you angry?" I didn't have an answer.

We called my maths teacher, who read the local news. He said the video was from years ago, somewhere else entirely. That night, two streets away, a man was beaten because someone believed the same forward.

I never forgot. When something makes you furious that fast, Vikas, it was probably made to. Stop. Check. Then decide.

qa.q: Who stopped young Uday from sharing the forward?
qa.a: Vikas's Nani stopped him; she was watching over his shoulder.

qa.q: What was young Uday feeling when he read the forward?
qa.a: He felt furious, his blood boiling, and was sure it was true.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Uday Mama's story, and why?
qa.a: Nani's questions about who sent it, where it was filmed and why it wanted him angry were the turning point, because they made him check before sharing.

qa.q: What happened to the man two streets away, and what does it show?
qa.a: He was beaten because someone believed the same forward, showing how outrage content can lead to real harm.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how a forwarded video pushed him to hate a group and share outrage, and learning to pause and verify because such content is built to anger.
